Summary
- Abri du Cap-Blanc (Cap-Blanc rock shelter) is a major Upper Paleolithic (Magdalenian) decorated rock shelter in the Vézère Valley, Dordogne, southwestern France.
- It is famous for a long sculpted frieze in high relief carved directly from the limestone shelter wall — primarily bison, plus horses and other figures — and is one of the rare examples of large Palaeolithic sculpture in situ.
- It is protected and presented as a musée-site and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage ensemble “Prehistoric Sites and Decorated Caves of the Vézère Valley.”

Location and setting
- The shelter is in the commune of Marquay (near Les Eyzies-de-Tayac) on the Vézère river valley in the Dordogne department (Périgord).
- It is an open rock shelter (abri), not a deep cave: the decorated frieze is on an exposed rock face under a protective overhang.

The art: what it is and how it looks
- The principal feature is a continuous sculpted frieze roughly 13 m long (estimates vary) containing about a dozen to a dozen-and-a-half animal figures carved in relief from the limestone.
- Bison are the dominant motif; there are also horses and possibly other ungulates. One of the bison figures (a recumbent bison) is particularly large and detailed.
- The figures are carved in high relief (i.e., shaped and modeled out of the living rock) and include incised details (lines for fur, hooves, eyes) and in some places traces of pigment have been reported.
- The artists used the natural contours of the rock in modeling forms and combined carving and engraving techniques. The work demonstrates advanced three-dimensional representation unusual for Paleolithic rock art, which more often is painted or engraved on flat walls.

Chronology and cultural attribution
- The frieze is generally attributed to the Upper Paleolithic, specifically the Magdalenian culture (roughly 17,000–12,000 years before present; typical datings for the Magdalenian are often placed roughly 15,000–12,000 BP). Precise radiocarbon dates for the frieze itself are difficult to obtain, so broader Magdalenian attribution is commonly used.
- Archaeological deposits in the shelter include Magdalenian habitation layers, which supports this attribution.

Discovery, research and conservation
- The frieze was recognized and studied by early 20th-century prehistorians; it has since been the subject of detailed archaeological and conservation work.
- Because it is an exposed shelter, conservation concerns (weathering, biological growth, visitor impact) are significant. The site has been stabilized and is managed as a museum with protective measures to limit deterioration while allowing public viewing.
- Abri du Cap-Blanc is included in the UNESCO World Heritage listing for the Vézère Valley prehistoric sites (inscribed in 1979), reflecting its outstanding universal value for understanding Paleolithic art and life.

Public access and presentation
- The site is a managed visitor attraction (musée-site) open to the public with access infrastructure (walkways, interpretive panels) so visitors can view the frieze without touching it.
- Interpretive materials usually place the frieze in the context of Magdalenian lifeways and Paleolithic art traditions of the Vézère Valley.

Significance
- Cap-Blanc is one of the most important examples of Palaeolithic relief sculpture — a relatively rare technological/artistic choice compared with the more common parietal paintings and engravings of the period.
- It contributes essential evidence about Paleolithic animal depiction, artistic technique, and the visual culture of Magdalenian hunter-gatherers in western Europe.
- Its preservation and display have made it an important educational resource and a focal point for public appreciation of Ice Age art.

What is debated or uncertain
- Exact dating of the carved frieze: the assignment to the Magdalenian is well supported by associated deposits and stylistic elements, but absolute dating of carvings themselves is inherently difficult.
- Some details of authorship, sequence of carving, and any potential polychromy (original colorings) are debated among specialists because of weathering and historical interventions.

If you want more
- I can provide:
  - References to key scholarly works and excavation reports (names, dates, publications).
  - Photographs, sketches, or a map showing the shelter’s location.
  - More detailed technical information about the carving techniques and conservation measures.
  - Visiting information (hours, ticketing) if you plan a trip.
